name: Dusty sienna
lede: Dusty sienna renders Chōjicha (丁子茶), a traditional Japanese name meaning "clove-brown", after cloth dyed with clove.

sections.title: Named for the clove
sections.body:
Our color library gives the source as 丁子茶 (Chōjicha), "clove-brown": chōji is the clove, long used in East Asian dyeing and incense, and cha again does double duty for both brown and tea [1]. No first-recorded date survives in our sources, so when the name entered use is undocumented here [1]. The library's own near-duplicate note pairs it with a second traditional name, Fushizome (柴染), "brushwood-dyed", at a color distance of just 2.0 [1].

The nearest named color in our graph is [[polished-brown]], at a color distance (ΔE2000) of 2.8, a more vivid shade; [[auburn]] sits 3.8 away and reads duller [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this brown in 1,673 of 23,781 paintings, about 7.0 percent, as photographed [3]. It is strongest well outside Japan: Tibetan painting carries it at over six times the overall rate, and Nepali work at close to four times [3]. The earliest dated appearance in the archive is a funerary papyrus from around 1069 BCE, over two millennia before the Japanese name on record; this is a floor set by what survives and was photographed, not a first sighting [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; the match is computed, not a pigment identification [3].
